extracted.intended_audience: prospective middle grades mathematics teachers, course instructors, and teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and teaching a college-level course (or professional development institute) in probability and statistics for prospective middle grades teachers, including course content, pedagogy, assessments, and final projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect students to explore connections and identify relevant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to explore the connections [among references and problems] and to decide, after reading the reference materials, what information about the movie would be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage student exploration of references; students must determine themselves which pieces of information are pertinent to solving an open-ended problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand expected value in relation to frequencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to understand how the expected value relates to frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material and preceding problems (e.g., coin-toss exercises) are used to connect theoretical probability to experimental frequency; instructors should sequence tasks to build this connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indicator-variable coding for events (0/1) to compute proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign numerical values 1 for head and 0 for tail so that the mean of the values equals the proportion of heads among tosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model events as 1 (occurs) / 0 (does not occur) to interpret sample means as proportions; use this coding to link single-trial expectation to sample proportions via law of large numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework problems are foundational, not supplemental
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework problems are considered foundational, rather than supplemental to the development of the course; students are asked to look for and build on connections among the problems, and are cautioned not to skip any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design homework so it supports and furthers course development; emphasize interconnectedness and require students attempt every problem to support in-class discussion and later assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor's guide purpose and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An instructor's guide is provided to give technical guidance so that student discussions may be appropriately directed by the instructor and to provide insight as to why the problem was written; it is not a solutions manual nor material to be shared with students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the guide to direct discussions and clarify instructor intent; do not distribute instructor notes to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply expected-value calculations with appropriate population adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating rare-event counts (e.g., deaths during a movie), compute individual expected values (e.g., 1/(number of 2-hour intervals in 75 years)) and scale by attendance while adjusting for differences between the movie-going population and the general population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how naive applications can overestimate/underestimate; discuss demographic differences (elderly, health) and why raw scaling may be inappropriate; use this as an example of careful model assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against blindly applying statistical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Many problems in life do not lend themselves to statistical analysis; the text includes frequent cautionary remarks and examples demonstrating the pitfalls of blindly applying statistical methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to evaluate applicability of statistical tools, to question assumptions, and to discuss weaknesses of statistical arguments (e.g., coincidental clustering versus evidence of causality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project: empirical statistical study expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students decide on a population and research question, design a survey or data collection method, gather data under several numerical and categorical variables, analyze using course techniques (regression, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing), and write a paper summarizing findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should include design, data collection, appropriate analysis, interpretation, and written communication; instructors should ensure use of methods taught in course and discuss limitations and biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project: analysis of a game of chance using simulation and theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Students analyze a game of chance (e.g., Craps) using both large-scale simulations and theoretical probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require students to answer probability questions via simulation and analytic methods, comparing results and discussing approximation/error and underlying assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group project: educational research and interview protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Students read educational research, design interview protocols to assess children's probabilistic misconceptions, interview twelve children, create a poster summarizing results, and share findings in a class-wide poster session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize research design, ethical data collection with children, qualitative analysis of misconceptions, and public presentation of findings (poster session).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment components (multiple modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are assessed via written exams, homework, group projects, and class participation; some instructors may collect and grade homework or grade it indirectly through exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of assessment types to measure conceptual understanding, problem-solving, application, and participation; clarify how homework contributes to grades (directly or via exam content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam problems follow from homework and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Exam problems might follow up on Class Activity discussions or on concepts from the reading (example: follow-up Enigma/plugboard counting problems; confidence interval conceptual question).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exams to assess deep understanding and carry-over from homework and class activities; include conceptual as well as computational questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class participation expectations (substantive engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely attending class is not enough. By participation, the instructor expects students to have completed the assigned reading every night, and to have attempted every homework problem that was assigned. Participation is judged based on involvement in class discussions and evidence that the student worked hard on homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grade participation on active contributions, engagement in group work, and preparedness (reading/homework attempts). Make expectations explicit and observable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre- and post-assessments to measure growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: pre and post-assessments are used to assess content and pedagogy understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administer content-and-pedagogy pre-tests at course start and post-tests at course end to document learning gains; use results to inform instruction and course revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem solving through multiple approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: problem solving through multiple approaches is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that admit multiple solution strategies, encourage comparison of approaches, and value diverse reasoning paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activities that integrate more than one mathematics content area
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: activities that involve more than one mathematics content area (e.g., links between geometry and algebra) are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create tasks that reveal connections across strands to build teachers' ability to connect curriculum topics for middle-level students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educator sharing of solutions and teaching strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: educator sharing of problem solutions and of teaching strategies with the whole group and in smaller grade-level groups and study groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure time for whole-class sharing and grade-level breakout discussions so teachers exchange practical classroom strategies and solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative assessment, including exit questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: formative assessment practices such as exit questions (used twice a day) and daily feedback are employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model formative assessment techniques instructors can use in their classrooms; collect daily feedback to adjust instruction and monitor understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: differentiating instruction to meet diverse learner needs is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide varied entry points and extensions for tasks so teachers learn to adapt lessons for heterogeneous middle level classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address students' mathematics language issues using graphic organizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: addressing students’ mathematics language issues, especially through the use of graphic organizers (e.g., concept maps, cluster-word webs, Frayer Model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use and model graphic organizers to clarify terminology and conceptual relationships; show teachers how to adapt these tools for middle-grade learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final projects as classroom-based action research
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: final projects that involve action research in educators’ classrooms (e.g., administer pre-tests, analyze student work, design instruction based on findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require projects to investigate actual students' learning, include data collection and analysis, and produce practical instructional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive use of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: extensive use of technology (graphing calculators, Internet data sources, applets, Geometer's Sketchpad) is integrated into courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technology to model investigations, provide manipulatives and data access, and to demonstrate tools teachers can use in their classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of student work
rubrics_metrics.description: Common course feature: regular review, analysis of student errors and misconceptions, and discussion of how this might inform instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include structured activities for analyzing authentic student responses and designing targeted follow-up instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster a dynamic, constructivist classroom through investigations and manipulatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The course models a dynamic, constructivist classroom by developing activities that lend themselves to investigation, sharing of strategies, and multiple approaches; integrate hands-on experiments and manipulatives wherever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and model inquiry-based tasks and use manipulatives to support conceptual understanding and collaborative problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize collaborative discussion structures (study groups and grade-level groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate collaboration with mixed-grade study groups (daily hour to discuss assignments and exit questions) and grade-level groups (perform grade-specific tasks and discussions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regular small-group structures to encourage peer support, reflection on readings, and grade-appropriate adaptation of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance mathematics content knowledge and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Course design emphasis: mathematics content knowledge and pedagogy are of primary importance, and one area should not dominate the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure course activities develop both deep mathematical understanding and practical pedagogical strategies; link content explorations to classroom teaching practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure teachers' content knowledge exceeds the level they teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should have depth of mathematical understanding that significantly exceeds the level at which they are teaching (e.g., teacher of function machines should understand linear functions deeply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities for teachers to explore richer mathematics (conceptual, historical, advanced examples) that they can simplify for middle level students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align courses with state grade level expectations and national standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Course components are aligned with statewide grade level expectations and national standards (e.g., NCTM), and courses address specific grade-level expectations for grades 5–9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map syllabus and activities to standards; document how course content supports licensure and grade-level expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify adult learning materials for middle level students
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult learning materials, intended to strengthen educators’ mathematical understanding, must be modified for use with middle level students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an activity uses advanced mathematics (e.g., Eratosthenes' circumference calculation), discuss and model how to adapt complexity and scaffolding for middle grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final project specifications for Proportional Reasoning (three required components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications: (1) Create and administer a pre-test to assess students' proportional reasoning; analyze results and summarize findings and instructional implications. (2) Select one pre-test item and pieces of student work illustrating a variety of responses; discuss numerical relationships, context, and follow-up questions. (3) Choose three students (different readiness levels) and create a display of their pre-assessment work; discuss levels of reasoning and instructional plans to address needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects must include concrete student data, analysis across levels, instructional implications, and artifacts (displays) suitable for sharing; use as capstone to demonstrate ability to assess and inform instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course grading policy and weightings (example syllabus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllabus example: Attendance/Participation 20% (participation requires completed reading and attempted homework), Two group projects 15% each, Two exams 25% each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit grade weightings and explain participation criteria; communicate exam schedule and project expectations in syllabus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading scale mapping percentages to letter grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Grading scale (after rounding to nearest percent): 93–100% A; 90–92% A-; 87–89% B+; 83–86% B; 80–82% B-; 77–79% C+; 70–76% C; 67–69% C-; 60–66% D; below 60% F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish a clear grading scale in the syllabus so students understand percentage-to-letter mappings.
